c.tagline: Transylvania's fairy-tale medieval hub, gateway to Bran Castle and the Carpathians.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed taxis are legally required to run a meter; confirm the driver starts it, and prefer companies with a visible name, phone number, and rate card on the door to avoid tourist overcharging.

emergency.note: 112 is Romania's unified emergency number for police, ambulance, and fire, with English-speaking operators generally available.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Brown bears wander the forested edges of town and Tampa trails at dusk — never approach or feed them — and agree taxi fares from the station or use apps.

hood_desc: The pedestrian heart of Brașov around Piața Sfatului, the Black Church, and the colorful merchant houses; best for first-timers who want museums, restaurants, and the old city walls all within walking distance.

The old Romanian quarter just outside the medieval walls, entered through the Schei Gate, with narrow lanes and small churches; suits travelers wanting local atmosphere and history a few minutes from Council Square.
A quieter residential district on the western edge of the city, home to Brașov's oldest church, St. Bartholomew's; suits those wanting an authentic, low-key base with easy bus access to downtown.

Romania's best-known ski and mountain resort, about 20 minutes from the city center via the Postăvarul cable car and slopes; suits travelers focused on skiing, hiking, or hotel spas over city sightseeing.

A large residential and commercial district south of downtown with shopping centers and everyday local life; suits budget travelers and longer stays wanting proximity to shops and transit at lower prices than the old town.

water.note: Mountain-sourced tap water is safe to drink.

transit.hours: Buses and trolleybuses generally run from about 5:00 AM to 11:00 PM.
transit.pay: Contactless bank card tap-on-board or a reloadable Brașov transit card; single-ride tickets can also be bought via SMS or the RATBV app.
transit.note: Brașov's public transit is run by RATBV using buses and trolleybuses; there is no metro or tram network, and the historic Old Town core is walkable without transit.

train: Brașov Railway Station (CFR main line hub)
bus: Intercity/maxi-taxi coaches to Bucharest, Sibiu, and Sighișoara

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus to city center

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up the bill or leaving about 10% at restaurants for good service is common and appreciated.

landmarks: Black Church (Biserica Neagră)
Southeastern Europe's largest Gothic church, smoke-darkened by a 1689 fire, shelters a famed Anatolian carpet collection and a mighty 4,000-pipe organ.
Council Square (Piața Sfatului)
Ringed by pastel merchant houses and the trumpet-towered Council House, Brașov's medieval marketplace is the postcard heart of the old Saxon town.
Mount Tâmpa
A cable car or forest trail climbs to the Hollywood-style Brașov sign, where the summit terrace overlooks red rooftops cupped by Carpathian ridges.
Catherine's Gate (Poarta Ecaterinei)
The only original medieval gate surviving, a 1559 fairy-tale tower with four corner turrets that once signified the town's right to capital punishment.
Rope Street (Strada Sforii)
Barely 1.3 meters wide, one of Europe's narrowest streets squeezes photogenically between medieval houses, a former firefighters' passage turned selfie magnet.
Weavers' Bastion (Bastionul Țesătorilor)
The best-preserved bastion of Brașov's medieval walls houses a museum with a remarkable scale model of the seventeenth-century fortified town.
St Nicholas Church and First Romanian School
In the Șchei quarter, this soaring Orthodox church adjoins the museum school where the first Romanian-language books were printed in the 1500s.
White Tower (Turnul Alb)
A steep stair climbs to this semicircular fifteenth-century watchtower for the classic panorama across the old town's rooftops to Mount Tâmpa.
Brașov Citadel (Cetățuia de pe Strajă)
A 16th-century hilltop fort built by Saxon settlers, now a free viewpoint over the old town's red rooftops and the surrounding Carpathian peaks.
Șchei District
The historic Romanian quarter once barred from the walled Saxon city, a maze of narrow lanes, old wooden houses and steep cobbled streets below Mount Tâmpa.

train.note: Brașov is the busiest junction in Transylvania and every international train between Budapest or Vienna and Bucharest calls at its single main station, about 2 km north of the old town (bus 4 or a short taxi ride). Domestic InterCity trains reach Bucharest in roughly 2 hr 30 min to 3 hr and Sighișoara in about 2 hours, and the Prahova Valley run through Sinaia and Bușteni is one of Romania's most scenic. International tickets sit on a separate fare system from domestic ones and are sold through bileteinternationale.cfrcalatori.ro or the partner railway rather than the ordinary CFR booking page; the booking window opens about two months out and sleeper berths on the Ister and Dacia go early in summer. Romania joined the Schengen area for land borders on 1 January 2025, so systematic passport checks at Curtici have eased, but carry your passport or ID card anyway.

intl.to: Budapest, Vienna, Munich, Milan & other Western European cities

bus.note: Brașov has three bus stations: Autogara 1 sits next to the railway station and handles most long-distance and international departures, while Autogara 2 and 3 mainly serve the surrounding Țara Bârsei villages and the Bran-Moeciu road. FlixBus and Romanian coach firms such as Normandia and Atlassib run to Hungary, Austria, Germany and Italy, serving Romania's large diaspora, and tickets are cheapest online. Domestically, minibuses to Bran Castle, Râșnov and Poiana Brașov leave frequently from Autogara 2, and coaches to Bucharest take about 3 hours. Border formalities on the Hungarian crossing are now light but drivers still collect ID at the frontier.

ferry.note: Brașov lies inland in a mountain basin roughly 200 km from the Black Sea with no navigable river, so there are no passenger boat or ferry services of any kind.

half.name: Bran Castle
half.blurb: Thirty minutes away, the clifftop fortress marketed as Dracula's castle bristles with towers, secret stairways and Queen Marie's surprisingly cozy royal interiors.

half.name: Râșnov Fortress
half.blurb: A hilltop peasant citadel from the 1200s crowns the village of Râșnov, its whitewashed walls sheltering lanes and views across the Burzenland plain.
